lines: This tower started tipping over about eight hundred fifty years ago. It still hasn't fallen. Here's why.
Pisa sits on soft clay and sand. And this tower, nearly fifteen thousand tonnes, got a foundation just three meters deep.
Step one: in eleven seventy-three, a ring of white marble rises. Five years later, at the second floor, the soft south side sinks. The lean begins.
Step two: do nothing. War stops the work for most of a century, and that pause saves it. The soil settles and gets stronger.
Step three: in twelve seventy-two, builders make the new floors taller on the sinking side. So the tower doesn't just lean. It curves.
But it kept moving. By nineteen ninety, the tilt hit five and a half degrees. Engineers shut it, roped it with steel cables, and stacked lead on the high side.
Then the clever part. Angled drills reached under the high side and pulled out soil, bit by bit. The ground sank, and the tower slowly tipped back.
Thirty eight cubic meters of soil. That was enough to undo about half a degree. Engineers say it's now stable for at least two hundred years.
